english.overview: Rabbi Sacks sees Parashat Vayetzei as framed by two journeys of Jacob: his flight from Esau to Laban, and his flight from Laban for home. The first three essays take Jacob's vision of a ladder between earth and heaven as a metaphor for prayer: prayer as an encounter that God initiates, as a structure of ascent and descent, and as a silencing of the "I". The fourth is about Jacob's love for Rachel and the lesson that love needs justice. The fifth looks at Leah and shows that God loves those who feel unloved, and that we must learn to listen to them.

essays.title: Encountering God
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Genesis; The Book of the Beginnings, Vayetzei, Encountering God
essays.summary:
Rabbi Sacks begins with Jacob alone at night, fleeing Esau, who lies down and sees a ladder with angels ascending and descending. The sages say that on the strength of this passage "Jacob instituted the evening prayer", reading vayifga as "he prayed" and bamakom, "the place", as God. So the three daily prayers belong to the three patriarchs: Abraham is morning, the beginner who broke his father's idols; Isaac is afternoon, the quiet courage of continuity, who re-digs his father's wells; Jacob is night, the man who discovers God in the midst of fear and who does not let go. If Abraham is originality and Isaac continuity, Jacob is tenacity.

Then he raises a difficulty: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the evening prayer is not obligatory. Tradition answers that this view follows those who base prayer on the Temple sacrifices, that Jacob was on a dangerous journey and so exempt, and that the sun set suddenly so he had not meant to pray at night. The deeper answer lies in the verbs. Abraham sought God, Isaac's prayer was a conversation, but Jacob did not initiate anything: he encountered God unexpectedly, as we meet a familiar face in a crowd. Such an experience cannot be made an obligation. It comes at night, when we are alone, afraid and vulnerable, and it leaves us saying that God was there all along and we were looking elsewhere.

questions.text: Why was the evening prayer, said to be Jacob's, not held to be obligatory like the prayers of Abraham and Isaac?
questions.quote: Why, if it was instituted by Jacob, was it not held to carry the same obligation as the prayers of Abraham and Isaac?

blocks.text: The sages say Jacob instituted the evening prayer, reading vayifga as praying and the place as God.
blocks.quote: On the basis of this passage the sages assert that

blocks.text: Each patriarch gives a weekday prayer its character: Abraham morning, Isaac afternoon, Jacob night.
blocks.quote: Abraham represents morning. He is the initiator

blocks.text: Isaac is the bridge of continuity, and Jacob the man who does not let go.
blocks.quote: Jacob is night. He sees his great vision of the ladder and angels at night.

blocks.text: Tradition gives three reasons why the evening prayer is not obligatory, including the sudden sunset.
blocks.quote: Tradition offers three answers.

blocks.text: The deeper reason: Abraham sought God and Isaac conversed with Him, but Jacob was met by God, unplanned.
blocks.quote: Jacob literally “encounters” God as we can sometimes encounter a familiar face among a crowd of strangers.

blocks.text: Where it lands: prayer is also openness and vulnerability, as God can take us by surprise.
blocks.quote: Prayer is not always predictable, a matter of fixed times and daily obligation.

essays.title: The Ladder of Prayer
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Genesis; The Book of the Beginnings, Vayetzei, The Ladder of Prayer
essays.summary:
Jacob, having left home, is in liminal space, between the home he flees and the destination he has not reached, and it is there, alone at night, that he dreams of the ladder. Rabbi Sacks reads the vision as the encounter between the human soul and God that later generations call prayer; the Zohar identifies the ladder with prayer, and the "house of God" becomes the synagogue. His proposal is that the vision shaped the structure of Jewish liturgy itself: a symmetrical pattern of ascent, standing in the Presence, and descent.

He shows it at three scales. Shaharit opens with pesukei dezimra as preparation, moves to the Shema and Amida, and ends with concluding hymns including Ashrei, following the Talmud's pious men who waited an hour, prayed an hour and waited an hour. The Amida moves from praise through request to thanks, with three steps forward and three back. The kedusha appears three times, and Maimonides explains that the first and third describe what the angels do while the middle one enacts it. Prayer is thus a ladder of words, thoughts and emotions on which we leave earth's gravitational field, stand before God, and return changed, bringing a fragment of heaven down to earth.

questions.text: What does Jacob's ladder vision signify?

blocks.text: The Zohar identifies the ladder with prayer, and the house of God comes to mean the synagogue.
blocks.quote: The Zohar (I, 201b) identifies the ladder in Jacob’s vision with prayer

blocks.text: Jewish liturgy has a three-part structure: ascent, standing in the Presence, descent.
blocks.quote: (a) ascent, (b) standing in the Presence, (c) descent

blocks.text: The same pattern shows in shaharit, in the Amida with its three steps forward and back, and in the kedusha.
blocks.quote: The three-fold pattern of shaḥarit is repeated in the microcosm in the structure of the Amida.

blocks.text: Where it lands: the third stage brings a fragment of heaven down to earth.
blocks.quote: then the third is bringing a fragment of heaven down to earth

essays.title: When the "I" is Silent
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Genesis; The Book of the Beginnings, Vayetzei, When the "I" is Silent
essays.summary:
Rabbi Sacks returns to Jacob's dream and notices a nuance lost in translation. Waking, Jacob says "ve'anokhi lo yadati", literally "and I, I knew it not", and the word anokhi, "I", is superfluous. Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz answers that we come to know that God is in this place by "not knowing the I": we know God when we forget the self.

This, he says, answers the great questions about prayer: does it change God, and does it contradict doing God's will? Prayer has two dimensions. One is mysterious: there are too many cases of answered prayer to deny that it changes our fate, and he tells of a man in a Nazi camp who lost the will to live, poured out his heart, and was next day transferred to the kitchen, where potato peelings kept him alive. The other is not mysterious: prayer changes us. Lehitpalel is reflexive, literally "to judge oneself", and prayer is where the "I" falls silent and we see we are not the centre of the universe. Then we notice the miracles of creation, revelation and redemption, and ask not what we need from life but what life needs from us. Prayer is an act of listening, and in the silence of the "I" we meet the "Thou" of God.

questions.text: Why does the text say "and I, I knew it not", with a superfluous "I"?
What does prayer actually do, given that God does not change?
questions.quote: What really happens when we pray?

blocks.text: The word anokhi, I, is superfluous in Jacob's words on waking.
blocks.quote: Anokhi means “I,” which in this sentence is superfluous.

blocks.text: Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz: we know God when we forget the self.
blocks.quote: We know God when we forget the self.

blocks.text: Prayer has a mysterious dimension, shown by the story of the man in the death camp.
blocks.quote: Prayer has two dimensions, one mysterious, the other not.

blocks.text: Prayer also changes us: lehitpalel is reflexive, and the "I" falls silent.
blocks.quote: The Hebrew verb lehitpalel, meaning “to pray,” is reflexive

blocks.quote: What does life need from me?

blocks.text: Where it lands: in the silence of the "I", we meet the "Thou" of God.
blocks.quote: In the silence of the “I,” we meet the “Thou” of God.

essays.title: On Love and Justice
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Genesis; The Book of the Beginnings, Vayetzei, On Love and Justice
essays.summary:
Jacob's love for Rachel begins at a well, where he rolls the stone off alone, kisses her and weeps. He serves seven years that "seemed to him but a few days", and this is the first time in the Torah that beauty is a reason for love and marriage. Then Laban substitutes Leah in the dark, answering "It is not done in our place to give the younger before the firstborn". Jacob marries Rachel too, but the lasting result is tragedy: Rachel has beauty, Leah has children, each is a source of pain to the other, and the conflict reaches the next generation in Joseph.

Rabbi Sacks weighs possible messages: Laban's cunning, a basis for the law in Leviticus, a punishment for following his eyes. He prefers another: the language echoes Jacob's own deception of Isaac (rimitani, mirma, tza'ir). The story is midda keneged midda, measure for measure, as the midrash has Leah retort "Is there a master without students?" There is a deeper principle too. "Love" appears three times for Rachel and three for Joseph, and Jacob later says "Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life". Love alone leaves the less loved feeling unloved. Against the contrast of a "God of love" and a "God of justice", he concludes that the covenant rests on both, for without justice love is blind and without love justice is cold.

questions.text: What is the message of the story of Jacob, Leah and Rachel?
questions.quote: What is unclear is its message.

blocks.text: Jacob meets Rachel at a well, rolls the stone away, and the text implies love at first sight.
blocks.quote: Jacob went near and rolled the stone from the well’s mouth

blocks.text: Jacob is in love with Rachel's beauty, the first time beauty is linked to love and marriage in the Torah.
blocks.quote: This is the first time physical beauty is associated with love and a reason for marriage.

blocks.text: Laban substitutes Leah at night, and the result is lingering tragedy between the sisters.
blocks.quote: Each wife is a source of pain to the other

blocks.text: The words used echo Jacob's own deception of Isaac, pointing to measure for measure.
blocks.quote: midda keneged midda, measure for measure

blocks.text: Love appears three times for Rachel and three for Joseph, and love alone leaves the less loved feeling unloved.
blocks.quote: Love is not enough, for it leaves the less loved feeling unloved

blocks.text: Where it lands: the covenant rests on love and justice together.
blocks.quote: For without justice, love is blind; and without love, justice is impersonal and cold.

essays.title: Hearing the Torah
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Genesis; The Book of the Beginnings, Vayetzei, Hearing the Torah
essays.summary:
Rabbi Sacks begins with keriat haTorah: the verb likro means "to call", not just "to read", and the Torah is meant to be proclaimed and heard, as in the hakhel ceremony and Ezra's reading in Nehemiah. Hearing differs from seeing because it unfolds in time, so a later word can overturn what we expected, as a punchline does in a joke. His example is in Vayetzei: after Jacob marries Rachel we hear "He also married Rachel, and he also loved Rachel", which suggests equal love, and then the next words, "more than Leah", crash the expectation. The grammar is broken, like a discord in a Mozart symphony. The next verse says "God saw that Leah was hated", which Ramban and Radak read as "relatively unloved". Leah's eyes were rakot, which Rashi and others take as easily moved to tears, and the names of her sons are cries to Jacob to see, to hear, to be attached to her.

Jacob is the patriarch of struggle and becoming, and "love" appears seven times in his story. He learns that love unites but also divides, and that love is not enough: we must heed those who feel unloved, which takes the ability to listen. Judaism is a religion of the ear, and the Shema, "Listen, O Israel", is that command, for those who wish to learn to listen to God must learn to listen to other people.

questions.text: What is going on in the drama between Leah and Jacob?
questions.quote: What is going on in this intense and sometimes tragic drama between Leah and Jacob?

blocks.text: Keriat haTorah means calling out the Torah, an experience of the ear rather than the eye.
blocks.quote: Keriat haTorah therefore means not reading, but proclaiming the Torah

blocks.text: Listening unfolds in time, so a later word can overturn what we expected.
blocks.quote: Listening is a process extended through time.

blocks.text: "He also married Rachel, and he also loved Rachel" is followed by "more than Leah", an ungrammatical shock.
blocks.quote: The next word sends our expectation crashing to the ground

blocks.text: Leah is described as hated, which means unloved, and her sons' names are pleas for Jacob's attention.
blocks.quote: Leah is pleading for attention.

blocks.text: Jacob stands for struggle and for becoming, and he loves more than any figure in Genesis.
blocks.quote: Jacob stands for becoming.

blocks.text: Where it lands: love is not enough, we must listen to the unloved, and that is the meaning of Shema Yisrael.
blocks.quote: love is not enough. We must also heed those who feel unloved.

hebrew.overview: הרב זקס מדגיש בפרשת ויצא שלושה נושאים. הראשון הוא חלום הסולם: יעקב פוגש את אלוהים דווקא בלילה, בבדידות ובפחד, ומכאן ירושתו של עם ישראל. השני הוא התפילה כסולם, שיש לה צורה של עלייה, עמידה וירידה. השלישי הוא סיפור יעקב, לאה ורחל, ממנו עולה שאהבה לבדה אינה מספיקה, ושצריך גם צדק ואוזן קשבת לאלה המרגישים לא אהובים.

essays.title: וכך נכנס האור
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Hebrew Edition, Vayeitze, 1
essays.summary:
הרב זקס שואל מדוע דווקא יעקב נקרא שם העם, והוא לא עזב את ארצו כאברהם, לא נעקד כיצחק ולא נלחם בעוול כמשה. התשובה, הוא אומר, רמוזה בחלום הסולם: יעקב בודד, בלילה, בורח מעשו, ושום דבר לא הכין אותו לפגישה. החזרה על ״וְהִנֵּה״ ועל ״וַיִּפְגַּע בַּמָּקוֹם״ מבטאת פגישה לא מתוכננת, ובלשון חז״ל המקום הוא הקב״ה. עם מאבקו הלילי במלאך יוצא שיעקב הוא האיש שחוויותיו הרוחניות העמוקות ביותר באות לו לבדו, בלילה, בלי שציפה להן, במרחב הלימינלי שבאמצע המסע.

כך גם עם ישראל, שפגש את אלוהים ״בְּאֶרֶץ מִדְבָּר״ ושרד גלות אחר גלות, וגילה שהשכינה עדיין בקרבו. דוד המלך קורא אל ה׳ מן המעמקים, ורבי נחמן מברסלב מורה לצעוק מעמקי הלב. הרב זקס מספר על אביו, שלא היה תלמיד חכם אך הלך זקוף כי הרגיש שה׳ איתו כשהתפלל או קרא תהלים. זו ירושתנו מיעקב: גם כשנפול, ניפול אל זרועותיו של אלוהים, ומבעד לסדק שבלב הנשבר, כדברי לאונרד כהן, נכנס האור.

questions.quote: למה יעקב? בקוראנו בסיפורי בראשית אנו שואלים זאת שוב ושוב.

blocks.quote: שימו לב לחזרה המרובעת על המילה

essays.title: סולם התפילה
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Hebrew Edition, Vayeitze, 2
essays.summary:
הרב זקס מפרש את חלום הסולם כמפגש בין אדם לאלוהים, מפגש שלימים ייוודע בשם תפילה ב״בית אלוהים״, והזוהר מזהה את הסולם עם התפילה. לדעתו החזון הזה אינו רק גרעין הרעיון אלא גם מקור להשפעה על תבניתה: בתפילה יש תבנית יסוד סימטרית של עלייה, עמידה לנוכח השכינה וירידה. שחרית פותחת בפסוקי דזמרה, מגיעה לקריאת שמע ולעמידה, ונגמרת בדברי תהילה, ובהם ״אשרי״ שנאמר גם בהתחלה. יסוד הדבר בברייתא שהמתפלל שוהה שעה לפני תפילתו ושעה אחריה.

אותו מבנה חוזר בתפילת העמידה: ברכות שבח הן הכנה, ברכות בקשה הן העמידה לפני המלך, וברכות הודיה הן הפרידה, ושלוש פסיעות קדימה ושלוש לאחור ממחישות זאת. גם בקדושה, הרמב״ם מסביר שהראשונה והשלישית מתארות מה שהמלאכים אומרים, והאמצעית משחזרת את מעשה האמירה. התפילה היא סולם של מילים, מחשבות ורגשות שבו נפרדים משדה הכבידה של הארץ, ואם עשתה את שלה אנו שבים אנשים אחרים. השלב השלישי הוא הורדת פיסת שמים אל הארץ, כי השמים יכולים להיות ממש כאן.

blocks.text: בתפילה יש תבנית שלושה חלקים: עלייה, עמידה לנוכח השכינה, וירידה.
blocks.quote: עלייה, עמידה לנוכח השכינה, וירידה

blocks.text: שחרית נפתחת בפסוקי דזמרה ונגמרת ב״אשרי״, על פי הברייתא.
blocks.quote: יסוד המבנה המשולש הזה הוא הברייתא

blocks.text: העמידה בנויה שבח, בקשה והודיה, עם שלוש פסיעות קדימה ושלוש לאחור.
blocks.quote: שלוש פסיעות קדימה בתחילת העמידה

blocks.text: הרמב״ם מבחין בין הקדושה שמתארת את המלאכים לקדושה שמשחזרת את מעשיהם.
blocks.quote: הקדושה הראשונה והשלישית הן הכנה לאירוע

blocks.text: המסקנה: השלב השלישי הוא הורדתה של פיסת שמים אל הארץ.
blocks.quote: הורדתה של פיסת שמים אל הארץ

essays.title: אהבה זה לא מספיק
essays.ref: Covenant and Conversation; Hebrew Edition, Vayeitze, 3
essays.summary:
הרב זקס פותח בכך שהיהדות היא דת של אהבה, ושלוש אהבות במרכזה: אהבת ה׳, אהבת הרע ואהבת הגר. היא גם הציוויליזציה הראשונה שהעמידה את האהבה במרכז החיים המוסריים, אך היא גם דת של צדק, ואברהם נבחר כדי שישמרו ״צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט״. מדוע נדרש שילוב של אהבה וצדק? התשובה בקטע קצר בפרשתנו, שמעוררת את מה שמבינים רק בשמיעה: ״וַיֶּאֱהַב גַּם אֶת רָחֵל״ מעורר ציפייה שהוא אוהב את שתיהן, והמילה ״מִלֵּאָה״ מפרה אותה בתחביר שבור שמבטא יחסים שבורים.

הפסוק הבא אומר ״שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה״, והיא הייתה אהובה פחות, אך הרגישה דחויה, וכאבה נשמע בשמות ילדיה. האהבה מאחדת אבל גם מפלגת, ובכל הופעה של השורש אה״ב בבראשית היא מחוללת עימות, מיצחק ועשו ועד יעקב ויוסף. לכן אי אפשר לבנות משפחה או חברה על אהבה לבדה: האהבה פרטיקולרית והצדק אוניברסלי, ושניהם נדרשים. כפי שאמר נילס בוהר, אפשר לראות מנקודת מבט של שופט או של אב, אך לא של שניהם יחד. הרב זקס מסיים: הבה נאהב, אך לא נשכח את אלה המרגישים לא אהובים.

questions.text: מדוע נדרש שילוב של אהבה וצדק, והאם אין די באהבה?
questions.quote: מדוע נדרש השילוב של אהבה וצדק? האם אין די באהבה?

blocks.text: היהדות היא דת של אהבה, ושל שלוש אהבות גדולות.
blocks.quote: היהדות היא דת של אהבה: של שלוש אהבות גדולות

blocks.text: ״וַיֶּאֱהַב גַּם אֶת רָחֵל מִלֵּאָה״ הוא תחביר שבור המבטא יחסים שבורים.
blocks.quote: התורה משתמשת במתכוון בתחביר שבור

blocks.text: לאה אהובה פחות ולכן מרגישה שנואה, וכאבה נשמע בשמות ילדיה.
blocks.quote: לאה לא הייתה שנואה. היא הייתה אהובה פחות.

blocks.text: האהבה מאחדת אך גם מפלגת, ובכל הופעה של השורש אה״ב בבראשית היא מחוללת עימות.
blocks.quote: האהבה מאחדת, אבל גם מפלגת

blocks.text: המסקנה: אהבה אינה מספיקה, ונדרש גם צדק, והבה לא נשכח את הלא אהובים.
blocks.quote: אבל אהבה אינה מספיקה
